purpose: Elotuzumab is used to treat multiple myeloma, which is a type of blood cancer that affects plasma cells in your bone marrow. It is used together with other cancer medicines, not on its own. It helps slow down or stop the cancer from growing and spreading.
how_it_works: Your immune system has special fighter cells called natural killer cells that help destroy harmful cells. Elotuzumab is a lab-made protein that attaches to a target found on both the cancer cells and your natural killer cells, bringing them together so your immune system can find and destroy the cancer cells more effectively. Think of it like putting a flag on the cancer cell so your body's defenders know exactly where to attack.
common_side_effects: Fatigue and tiredness, diarrhea, constipation, numbness or tingling in hands and feet, cough, decreased appetite, weight loss, fever, upper respiratory infections, and infusion reactions during or after the IV drip such as chills, flushing, or low blood pressure.
warnings: You may have a reaction during the infusion, so you will be given pre-medications like steroids and antihistamines beforehand to reduce this risk. This medicine can increase your risk of infections, including serious ones. It can also raise your blood sugar levels, especially because of the steroid pre-medications given with it. Tell your doctor if you are pregnant, planning to become pregnant, or breastfeeding, as this medicine can harm an unborn baby. Regular blood tests will be needed to monitor your health during treatment.
typical_dosing: Elotuzumab is given as an intravenous (IV) infusion, meaning it goes directly into your vein at a clinic or hospital. The dose and schedule depend on which combination regimen your doctor prescribes, but it is commonly given once a week for the first two cycles and then once every two weeks or once a month afterward. Each infusion session can take several hours, so plan accordingly.
